newsitem.title: USA: Europe monetary union could disrupt global markets.
newsitem.headline: Europe monetary union could disrupt global markets.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The drive to create a zone of currency stability within Europe with the 1999 launch of monetary union could lead to greater volatility in foreign exchange markets outside, an IMF conference heard this week.

International Monetary Fund chief economist Michael Mussa told reporters Wednesday that conference participants mostly agreed that the ambitious project will begin on time with the introduction of a single European currency on Jan. 1, 1999.
But there were many concerns expressed about what that would mean for the world monetary system as a whole.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, for one, said that the advent of European monetary union could mean more global currency instability, not less.
"The incidences of (currency) misalignments could become more frequent and more damaging," he told the conference of academics, government and IMF officials.

That is because of an expected shift away from a world monetary system dominated by a single currency, the dollar, to a potentially more unstable one in which the new European currency, the euro, and the Japanese yen would play a bigger role.
Mussa said conference participants generally agreed that the euro is likely to be a relatively strong currency that will become a key rival to the dollar.

The markets have been abuzz recently with rumours that the Jan. 1, 1999 start of EMU will be delayed because of the difficulties that many countries, particularly Germany, face in meeting the budget criteria for this year set under the Maastricht Treaty on EMU.
Camdessus came out strongly at the conference against any delay and suggested that there was room for intepretation in the tough criteria to allow the ambitious project to go ahead.
But a senior German official said he could not exclude the possibility that the launch of European monetary union might be delayed. However, he added that he did not think that was likely.

"For me, the most likely outcome is that we will start on time," said Klaus Regling, Director General for European and International Financial Relations at the German Finance Ministry. "But we can't exclude the other possibility."
Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Paul Jenkins even argued that a delay in EMU would not necessarily disrupt financial markets if it were handled correctly.
"If a delay in the start of EMU is seen as supporting Europe's long-run economic fundamentals, it would not necessarily lead to financial instability," Jenkins said.

While there may not have been much public hand wringing at the conference over the threat of a delay to EMU, there was more than enough concern expressed about what its actual launch might mean for the markets and the world economy.

Fred Bergsten, who heads the Institute for International Economics think tank here, predicted a massive $500 billion to $1 trillion shift into euros over the next few years by governments and private investors.
"We will move quite promptly into a bipolar international monetary system," Bergsten said, adding, "The euro will be a strong currency from the outset."
He also argued that Europe will become more insular after EMU and thus more prone to "benign neglect" of its currency.
"The likelihood is increased volatility and potentially large misalignments from time to time," Bergsten said.

A senior U.S. Federal Reserve official voiced the opposite concern -- that the launch of EMU would lead to an excessive focus on currency policy within Europe, representing a "step backward" in economic policy coordination among major nations.
"One of the concerns ... is that the world will take a step backward to a world in which the focus will be on exchange rates rather than on the underlying economic and financial policies," he said.
